profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting at a large hospital's preventive cardiology service to align the cardiology and nursing workstreams before launching an expanded nurse-coordinated cardiovascular prevention pathway. The pathway is meant to support recently discharged patients with medication concordance, smoking cessation, diet and exercise counseling, and family-inclusive follow-up. The agenda is to confirm how referrals from cardiology will enter the program, what the nurse-led first contact will include, how progress will be documented in the shared record, and what materials will be handed to pharmacists and psychologists downstream. The expected outcome is a shared understanding of the handoff process for next week's pilot cohort, the status of the shared care-plan template, and who will update the prevention dashboard after initial patient contacts.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Consultant Cardiologist and Clinical Lead for Preventive Cardiology
members.expertise: Secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome, lipid management, discharge planning, multidisciplinary pathway design
members.background: Maya is an attending cardiologist who recently took over the hospital's cardiovascular prevention initiative after leading a post-MI discharge optimization project. She works closely with inpatient teams and is used to structuring care around discharge milestones and medically cleared plans.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to look tightly organized for an upcoming executive review, minimize post-discharge gaps attributed to cardiology, and avoid adding unbounded tasks to physician documentation time.
hidden_assumptions: A patient being 'enrolled' in the prevention pathway means cardiology has placed the referral order and the patient appears on the nurse worklist, even if direct patient contact has not yet occurred.
The 'baseline' for the prevention dashboard refers to discharge-day clinical data and medication list, because those are the most reliable hospital-verified starting values.
The shared 'care plan' covers the nurse-facing prevention goals and handoff notes, while detailed family engagement or community resource arrangements can sit outside the main template if needed.
When the team says the nurse will 'close the loop' after first contact, she assumes this means updating the EHR note and routing it to cardiology within the existing in-system workflow.

members.name: Sarah O'Neill
members.role: Advanced Practice Cardiovascular Prevention Nurse and Nurse Coordinator
members.expertise: Motivational interviewing, cardiac rehabilitation coordination, medication concordance support, family-centered self-management coaching
members.background: Sarah has spent eight years running nurse-led follow-up for heart failure and rehab referrals, with a strong focus on what patients understand and can realistically do once they are home. She often bridges hospital care with pharmacy, psychology, and community rehabilitation services.
members.private_state: She wants the pathway to protect meaningful patient engagement time, ensure family and behavioral issues are not treated as optional extras, and avoid being judged successful based on administrative completion rather than actual patient contact.
hidden_assumptions: A patient is not truly 'enrolled' until the nurse has spoken with the patient or family, explained the program, and confirmed participation in the first follow-up step.
The 'baseline' should be the information gathered at the first nurse contact after discharge, because discharge-day medication lists and intentions often change once the patient is home.
The shared 'care plan' should include barriers, family involvement, and referrals to pharmacy or psychology, because those are core parts of prevention rather than side notes.
When she says she will 'close the loop,' she assumes this includes calling the community pharmacist or rehab service if adherence barriers emerge, not just documenting internally.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss which patients will be 'enrolled' in the pilot by Friday
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means patients for whom the discharge referral order has been placed and routed into the prevention pathway worklist.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means patients whom the nurse has successfully reached, introduced the program to, and confirmed for active follow-up.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In care-pathway meetings, 'enrolled' sounds like standard operational language and both meanings imply patients are entering the program, so the term creates a natural but false sense of shared understanding.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'baseline' data will populate the dashboard
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use the patient's 'baseline' for tracking prevention progress
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the discharge packet baseline: discharge blood pressure, discharge medication list, smoking status recorded on the ward, and rehab referral status at discharge.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the first follow-up baseline: what medications the patient is actually taking at home, current smoking or diet behavior, and family-reported barriers captured during the first nurse call.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are referring to the same patient and same general idea of a starting point, and in routine clinical conversation 'baseline' is rarely unpacked unless a discrepancy has already caused trouble.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the shared care plan
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the nurse will update the 'shared care plan' after the first contact
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the shared care plan includes the standardized prevention template fields needed by cardiology: risk-factor checklist, medication issues, and next review date.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the shared care plan also includes family readiness, transport or affordability barriers, and whether psychology or pharmacy outreach has been initiated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe they are referring to the same institutional artifact and neither sees their interpretation as unusual; the disagreement concerns silent boundaries of inclusion rather than a visible disagreement about the artifact itself.

misalignment_points.topic: How to 'close the loop' on adherence concerns
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the nurse will 'close the loop' on any medication adherence issue that comes up
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects the nurse to document the issue in the EHR, send an in-system message back to cardiology, and let cardiology decide whether external follow-up is needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to directly contact the patient's pharmacist, rehab team, or family as part of resolving the issue before documenting the outcome.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase signals responsibility and follow-through without specifying workflow details, and both methods are professionally plausible enough that neither party feels a need to clarify in a short coordination meeting.

turns.inner_thought: I need this launch to sound clean and controlled for the executive review. The key is a simple handoff: cardiology places the referral order, the patient is enrolled, and the name lands on Sarah's worklist. Then after first contact the shared care plan should be updated in the standard template so our team can see what happened without adding another documentation burden for physicians.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Sarah. I wanted to use today to pin down the handoff for next week's pilot patients and make sure we're aligned on who is enrolled, how the shared care plan gets updated, and what goes downstream after the first contact.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as we protect real outreach time and don't reduce the pathway to names on a list. My first contacts need to cover what patients are actually doing at home, whether family is involved, and what support they need. And if problems come up, closing the loop means helping resolve them, not just filing a note.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I've been building the outreach schedule on the nursing side, and the first contacts will focus on medication concordance, lifestyle priorities, and any family support needs. After that I'll update the shared care plan and close the loop on anything that needs follow-through.

turns.inner_thought: If the fellows sign the remaining discharge referrals on time, we should have twelve patients enrolled by Friday. That gives me a defensible pilot denominator before anyone asks for numbers. From my perspective once the order is placed and they're on the prevention list, they're in.
turns.utterance: From the cardiology side, we should have twelve post-discharge patients enrolled by Friday once the referrals are signed and they're visible on the prevention list.

turns.inner_thought: Twelve is manageable if most of them answer or if I can reach family quickly. If they're enrolled by Friday, I should be able to get through first conversations with most of them by early next week and confirm who's really participating.
turns.utterance: Twelve sounds workable. I would expect most of those enrolled patients to have had their first phone contact by early next week, assuming we don't hit too many access issues over the weekend.

turns.inner_thought: For the dashboard, baseline needs to anchor to discharge status because that's the hospital-verified starting point and what leadership will want to compare against. If we drift away from discharge-day data, the pilot will look messy and hard to interpret.
turns.utterance: Great. On the reporting side, I'd like the prevention dashboard to use the patient's baseline for tracking progress, so at the executive review we can compare follow-up against where things stood at discharge.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, baseline should come from the first real conversation after discharge, because that's when we learn what survived the transition home. The discharge list is often aspirational. I'll enter what they're actually taking and the barriers they describe once I speak with them.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I'll populate the baseline during the first contact, and it'll actually be helpful because that's often when patients tell us what they're really taking once they get home.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the shared care plan is updated promptly with the standard prevention fields, cardiology can review quickly without digging through long narrative notes. I mainly need the risk-factor snapshot, medication questions, and next review date visible in one place.
turns.utterance: Perfect. And I'd like the shared care plan updated right after that first call so the cardiology team can quickly see the key risk factors, any medication questions, and the next review date.

turns.inner_thought: I'll do that, but for me the shared care plan has to be the real working document, not just a cardiology checklist. If family support is weak or transport and cost are the actual reasons rehab won't happen, those belong there too or the plan won't reflect reality.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll make sure the shared care plan captures family involvement, readiness to change, and any barriers that are affecting adherence or rehab attendance.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If adherence issues come up, the crucial thing is that the nurse closes the loop quickly inside the EHR so my team can see it and decide whether anything beyond cardiology messaging is needed. I don't want loose ends after discharge.
turns.utterance: And if any medication adherence issue surfaces, the main thing for me is that we close the loop promptly so nothing just sits unresolved after discharge.

turns.inner_thought: That's exactly the point. If there's an adherence issue, I'll sort it with whoever needs to be involved—pharmacy, rehab, family, sometimes psychology—so the patient isn't waiting for another internal handoff. Then I'll document the outcome.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can close the loop on those cases and keep things moving with pharmacy or other supports where needed.

turns.inner_thought: I need downstream teams to get what they need from the existing note structure, not through separate free-text updates that create duplicate work. If Sarah updates the shared care plan and routes it internally, pharmacy and psychology should be able to work from that.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. I also want to make sure psychology and pharmacy receive whatever they need from the first-contact notes without us creating duplicate documentation.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me, as long as the note is rich enough to reflect the real situation and not just tick-box completion. I'll work through the enrolled list as I define it through actual contact, update the shared care plan after each outreach, and enter baseline from those conversations for the pilot dashboard.
turns.utterance: Understood. So I'll work through the enrolled list, update the shared care plan after outreach, and feed baseline information into the dashboard for the pilot cohort.
